description: State changes, layering, threat escalation, intensity gating. Music that responds to gameplay states — from stealth to combat to victory, all within the same musical DNA.

coreIdentity: Music must support gameplay states — exploration, tension, combat, resolution — without jarring transitions between them
Intensity is gated — the music should be able to smoothly transition between 3-5 intensity levels
Loopability is essential — music must cycle seamlessly, with variation that doesn't sound repetitive over extended listening
Layering is the primary structural tool — add/remove layers to change intensity without changing the core pattern
The player's actions determine the music — not the other way around
creativeFocus: Vertical layering — 5-8 layers that can be independently muted/unmuted for real-time intensity changes
Loop fatigue prevention — techniques to keep a looping pattern interesting over 10+ minutes
Threat signaling — musical cues that communicate danger level without being distracting
Transition smoothness — crossfading between intensity states without audible seams
Hybrid palette — organic + synthetic, acoustic + electronic, real + unreal
commonMaterials: Percussion — ranging from sparse (stealth) to dense (combat), often with ethnic/world elements
Synth bass — for weight and threat, often distorted for high-intensity states
Orchestral elements (hybrid) — string stutters, brass stabs, processed orchestral textures
Drones — constant low texture for tension, can swell for threat escalation
Rhythmic pulses — short, percussive synth hits that create forward drive
arrangementLogic: Vertical arrangement — all layers share the same cycle length, intensity changes by adding/removing layers
Intensity levels: stealth (2-3 layers), tension (3-4 layers), combat_low (4-5 layers), combat_high (5-7 layers), climax (all layers)
Each intensity level adds specific layer types: stealth adds drum + drone, tension adds bass + pulse, combat adds full percussion + synth
Loop length: 4-8 cycles standard, with micro-variation to prevent fatigue
grooveLogic: Rhythm is the primary intensity driver — more percussion = higher intensity
Combat states use driving, forward-momentum rhythms
Stealth states use sparse, irregular percussion or none at all
Tension states use rhythmic pulses without full percussion — the 'about to engage' feel
timbreLogic: Dark, aggressive, but not harsh — the player needs to hear game audio clearly
Low-mid focus (100-500Hz) for weight and threat
High-frequency content is controlled — hi-hats, shakers, and high percussion should not mask game sound effects
Distortion increases with intensity — clean in stealth, heavily processed in combat
harmonicLogic: Dark modes — phrygian, locrian, harmonic minor
Pedal tones — a constant low note with changing harmonies above
No complex chord progressions — 1-2 chords, mostly drones with moving inner voices
Tritone intervals for threat and unease
spatialLogic: Mono compatibility is important — many players use TV/monitor speakers
Width increases with intensity — narrow and focused for stealth, wide for combat
Bass and kick always centered for impact
energyCurve: The energy curve follows gameplay, not musical structure
Ability to transition between any two intensity levels within 1-2 cycles
Peak energy reserved for boss fights and climactic moments
Recovery states (post-combat) should release tension without losing the dark atmosphere

gestureLibrary.name: Layer Stack for Intensity
gestureLibrary.description: Build a vertical stack of 5-8 layers where each layer represents an intensity threshold. Layers can be toggled in real-time to match gameplay state. The core pattern stays the same — only density changes.
useWhen: Need dynamic music that responds to gameplay
gestureLibrary.repair: Ensure each layer works in every possible combination. Test all layer permutations. The 'all layers' state must not clip or become muddy.
strudelHints: // Build all layers in one stack(). Use layer markers for game engine to toggle. Each layer is additive — they should all work together.

gestureLibrary.name: Threat Escalation Pulse
gestureLibrary.description: A rhythmic element that increases in speed and intensity as threat level rises. Starts as a slow pulse (1 hit per 2 cycles), escalates to rapid stutter (4-8 hits per cycle) at maximum threat.
gestureLibrary.repair: The escalation must be smooth — sudden speed changes are jarring. Use gradual .fast() or .slow() over 4-8 cycles.

gestureLibrary.name: Loop Fatigue Prevention
gestureLibrary.description: Techniques to keep a 4-8 cycle loop interesting over 10+ minutes of gameplay. Micro-variation, stochastic variation, and layer rotation keep the loop fresh without breaking the loop structure.
gestureLibrary.repair: Use .sometimesBy() on secondary elements to create variation. Rotate which percussion elements are playing. Slightly vary filter settings. Never change the core rhythm or harmonic structure — only the details.
strudelHints: // Variation technique: use .sometimesBy(0.15, ...) on secondary percussion, .lpf() with very slow modulation '<800 1200 800>'.slow(24) for subtle timbral shifts.

gestureLibrary.name: Combat Drop
gestureLibrary.description: The transition from tension/stealth to full combat. All combat layers activate within 1-2 cycles. A distinct musical 'hit' (orchestral impact, synth stab, drum fill) marks the transition.
avoidWhen: Stealth gameplay where sudden noise would be detrimental
Transitions should be subtle and unnoticeable
gestureLibrary.repair: The combat drop should feel powerful but not cheap. Use a low-frequency impact (not a high-frequency sting) for weight. Layer a short drum fill to bridge the transition.
strudelHints:
// Sting layer (triggered once at transition): s('metal:2').gain(0.7).room(0.3).decay(2).once()
// Then combat layers fade in over 1 cycle

gestureLibrary.name: Hybrid Percussion Layer
gestureLibrary.description: Combine orchestral percussion (taikos, frame drums) with electronic percussion (industrial hits, processed samples). The hybrid approach creates a unique, un-placeable sound — neither fully acoustic nor fully electronic.
useWhen: Standard drum kits sound too 'real world'
avoidWhen: The game setting is strictly realistic or strictly futuristic
gestureLibrary.repair: Process the acoustic elements with electronic techniques (distortion, filtering, reverb) so the hybrid blend is seamless.
strudelHints: // Layer acoustic-style and electronic percussion in separate layers. Process acoustic hits with .lpf().gain() modulation. Use .room() differently on each.

gestureLibrary.name: Tension Drone
gestureLibrary.description: A low, dark drone that gradually increases in presence during tension states. The drone may incorporate very slow beating patterns, subtle distortion increases, or filter openings that signal rising danger.
gestureLibrary.repair: The drone should never become foreground — it's a subliminal signal. If players consciously notice it, it's too loud.

gestureLibrary.name: Post-Combat Release
gestureLibrary.description: After combat ends, the music doesn't immediately return to exploration — it passes through a brief 'release' state. Layers drop away, reverb increases, the remaining elements are sparse and atmospheric.
useWhen: Transition to exploration or narrative moment
gestureLibrary.repair: The release should last 2-4 cycles. Keep the bass drone but reduce gain. Increase reverb on remaining elements. Remove all percussion except maybe a very sparse kick.
strudelHints: // Mute combat layers, keep drone, add reverb to remaining elements, reduce gain over 4 cycles.

gestureLibrary.name: Stealth Pulse
gestureLibrary.description: An extremely sparse, quiet rhythmic element for stealth states. 1-2 hits per cycle at most. The pulse suggests a heartbeat — the player character's tension made audible.
gestureLibrary.repair: Keep the pulse very quiet. It should be felt as tension, not heard as music. Use low-frequency sounds (low tom, muted kick, sub pulse).

antiCliches.symptom: The same taiko + ostinato strings + braaam formula used in every AAA game trailer. This signals 'generic game music' immediately.
antiCliches.repair: Develop a distinctive percussion identity for this specific game. Combine at least one unusual element (processed found sound, ethnic instrument, synthetic texture) with traditional percussion to create a unique hybrid palette.

antiCliches.symptom: The same 4-cycle loop plays unchanged for the entire gameplay sequence. Players will notice the repetition within 2-3 minutes and it becomes annoying.
antiCliches.repair: Add at least 3 layers of micro-variation: filter modulation, percussion variation (.sometimesBy()), and occasional extra hits. The loop's core identity stays the same but the surface details are constantly shifting.

antiCliches.symptom: Using only orchestral instruments (strings, brass, percussion) without any electronic or processed elements. This limits the game's sonic identity to 'movie music'.
antiCliches.repair: Blend in at least 2 electronic/synthetic elements: synth bass, processed textures, industrial percussion, or heavily processed samples. The hybrid approach creates a more distinctive and game-appropriate sound.

antiCliches.cliche: Sudden music cut on state change
antiCliches.symptom: Music abruptly stops or changes when gameplay state changes, creating jarring transitions. This breaks immersion and signals 'this is just background music'.
antiCliches.repair: Crossfade between intensity states over at least 1 cycle. Keep at least one element constant across all states (usually the drone or harmonic foundation) as a 'through-line'.

antiCliches.cliche: Combat music that overpowers game audio
antiCliches.symptom: Full-frequency, maximally dense combat music that masks important game audio cues (footsteps, enemy sounds, UI feedback).
antiCliches.repair: Carve out frequency space for game audio. Low-pass combat music below 100Hz for sub-bass game effects. Create a 'notch' around 1-3kHz for dialogue and UI sounds. Combat intensity should come from rhythmic density and timbral aggression, not sheer volume.

crossStyleBridges.keepFromBase: Intensity gating, vertical layering, loop structure
crossStyleBridges.borrowFromOther: Industrial percussion palette, hypnotic repetition, distortion/texture as intensity driver
crossStyleBridges.avoid: Don't let the techno influence create a dance-music feel. The groove should serve tension and combat, not dancing. Avoid four-on-the-floor kick patterns.
crossStyleBridges.resultIdea: Industrial combat music — dark, mechanical, relentlessly driving. Percussion is the primary intensity driver, with layers of metallic hits, distorted pulses, and sub-bass weight building through the intensity levels.
usefulWhen: Need more aggressive, less orchestral palette
crossStyleBridges.exampleConcept: Mech facility infiltration — stealth state: distant industrial pulses, metallic echoes; tension: rhythmic machinery sounds emerge, sub-bass starts; combat: full mechanical assault, distorted impacts, relentless percussion drive

crossStyleBridges.keepFromBase: Layered intensity system, dark harmonic palette
crossStyleBridges.borrowFromOther: Break slicing techniques for percussion variation, sub-bass weight, dub delay for spatial depth
crossStyleBridges.avoid: Keep tempo moderate (100-140 BPM) — jungle tempos (>150) are too fast for most game combat. Use break techniques at moderate speeds.
crossStyleBridges.resultIdea: High-intensity combat with jungle-inspired break manipulation — rapid percussion variation at moderate tempos, deep sub-bass for impact, dub-inspired spatial effects for otherworldly atmosphere.
crossStyleBridges.exampleConcept: Cybernetic assault — break-like percussion patterns at 130 BPM, sliced and rearranged in real-time, sub-bass impacts on major hits, the rhythm constantly shifting to match combat intensity

crossStyleBridges.borrowFromOther: Extreme spatial depth, very slow textural evolution, foreground/background ambiguity, near-silence as tension tool
crossStyleBridges.avoid: Don't let the ambient influence remove the rhythmic drive. Stealth states can be ambient-like but tension and combat states must retain forward momentum.
crossStyleBridges.resultIdea: Stealth music with genuine ambient depth — exploration states that are musically interesting in their own right, not just 'the quiet part before combat'. Tension builds through textural evolution rather than rhythmic escalation.
crossStyleBridges.exampleConcept: Deep station infiltration — exploration: vast, dark ambient textures, distant mechanical sounds, the station breathing; tension: textures slowly compress, filter openings reveal hidden frequencies, the silence between events becomes threatening

strudelIdioms.useCase: The vertical layering tool. 5-8 layers representing intensity levels. Layers must be designed to work together in any combination.
strudelIdioms.risk: Medium — must test all layer combinations for phase issues and clipping

strudelIdioms.useCase: Tempo. Game combat: 100-140 CPM. Faster = more intense but less weight. Choose tempo that works for both low and high intensity states.
Loop fatigue prevention. Apply to secondary percussion, filter modulation, extra hits. Probability 0.1-0.2 for subtle variation.
strudelIdioms.risk: Low — keep probability low to maintain loop coherence

strudelIdioms.useCase: For creating specific rhythmic patterns. Combat music benefits from precise, irregular rhythms — not simple grids.
strudelIdioms.example: s('bd').struct('x ~ ~ x ~ x ~ ~ ~ x ~ x ~ ~ x ~')

strudelIdioms.useCase: Filter for intensity control and frequency management. Lower lpf values for stealth (200-500Hz), higher for combat (1000-4000Hz). Use hpf to carve space for game audio.
strudelIdioms.example:
.lpf(300) // Stealth — dark and muffled
.lpf(3000) // Combat — open and aggressive

strudelIdioms.useCase: Layer balancing for intensity. Stealth layers: 0.05-0.15. Tension layers: 0.15-0.3. Combat layers: 0.3-0.7. Never exceed 0.95 total.
strudelIdioms.risk: Low — total gain must stay below 1.0

strudelIdioms.useCase: Spatial depth. Low room for combat (0.1-0.3) to maintain punch. Medium room for tension (0.3-0.6). High room for stealth (0.6-0.9) for atmosphere.
For pitched elements. Dark modes (phrygian, locrian). Pedal tones with moving inner voices. No chord progressions.
Intensity modulation. .fast() for combat fills and urgency. .slow() for stealth and tension states.
Stereo width for combat intensity. Use on synth and percussion layers to increase perceived width during combat states.

examplePatterns.title: Multi-Intensity Combat System
examplePatterns.whyUseful: Demonstrates the 5-tier intensity system with clear layer roles. Each layer group can be toggled independently for gameplay-responsive music.
warnings: All layers must be tested together for gain staging — remove layers until the full-combat state doesn't clip
Some layers may need frequency adjustments when combined

sourceNotes.title: Game Combat Style Definition
sourceNotes.note: Based on adaptive game music principles from titles like DOOM (2016), Hollow Knight, Hades, and Metal Gear Solid — emphasizing vertical layering, intensity gating, and hybrid orchestral/electronic palettes.
